# The Price of Thinking: Reasoning Effort as a Model-Specific API Contract

- **Authors**: Yeabin Moon
- **Venue**: cs.AI
- **Published**: 2026-08-16
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16956>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.16956v1>
- **Topics**: overthinking
- **Relevance score**: overthinking 0.50

## In one line

A preregistered, paired 360-call measurement on 30 AIME 2026 items of what a buyer gets by setting a reasoning-effort parameter explicitly versus omitting it on the same model, pricing every paid attempt including wrong and no-answer ones.

## Problem

The listed token price of a reasoning model is not the price of a completed task, because hidden thinking tokens are allocated before the visible answer and are billed. Prior work (Chen et al. 2026) established that realized cost misorders listed prices in about one in three of 336 model-task comparisons and that repeated calls to a fixed query vary substantially in cost, but it runs each model at a single reasoning setting, analyses cost separately from quality, and treats a paid attempt that returns no answer as a missing observation rather than a purchased outcome. That leaves unresolved what a buyer receives by moving one effort term while holding the model fixed, and whether two request surfaces exposing the same nominal control implement omission the same way. The paper argues the right unit is not the model name but the dated contract: requested and served model, effort term or its omission, output rail, service product, prompt, price schedule, and collection date.

## Contributions

- A registered within-model paired contrast isolating the reasoning-effort request term while holding model, prompt, items, rail, service product and price schedule fixed, with the item-clustered inference that repeated calls require.
- The measured result that explicitly setting high effort cost $0.01031 more per call [+$0.00204, +$0.01974] while the accuracy contrast +0.0133 [-0.0267, +0.0467] did not exclude zero.
- A frozen five-way terminal-outcome taxonomy that keeps wrong, no-answer and provider-failure calls inside the purchased outcome mixture and its cost total rather than dropping them as missing data.
- A dated contract census plus 19 preregistered raw-response probes showing that the meaning of omitting the effort parameter differs across models and within a single provider, with an evidence hierarchy that refuses to upgrade an indeterminate absent-thinking-block result.
- The argument that the priced unit is the dated API contract (requested and served model, effort term or omission, rail, service product, prompt, price schedule, date) rather than the model name.
- Preregistered item-count gates that refuse p99 and 90%-CVaR at n=30, and a conservative gate on rail-exhaustion claims that fired and narrowed the claim as specified.
- Cost accounting reconciled against authenticated provider console balances at cent granularity, with SHA-256-pinned immutable artifacts and a full $33.043144 spend disclosure.

## Method

A registered paired contrast run in one session on 2026-07-18: claude-sonnet-5 with explicit high effort against claude-sonnet-5 with the effort parameter omitted, 30 AIME 2026 items x 5 stateless calls each = 150 calls per cell, same frozen prompt template (aime_frozen_v1) and a 64,000-token output rail. Note the two cells do not differ in documented effort level: Sonnet 5's documented defaults are high effort and adaptive thinking, so the contrast is explicit-high versus defaulted-high, not high versus low. Single-pass reference cells add gpt-5.6-terra omitted and claude-fable-5 omitted (30 x 1 each), plus a non-contemporaneous 5-item gpt-5.4-mini low/high bridge from 2026-07-09. Every attempted purchase receives a delivered cost reconstructed from provider-reported usage under the registered price schedule (reconciled against console balance changes at cent granularity) and exactly one of five terminal categories under a frozen precedence rule: correct, wrong, no_answer_rail (rail exhausted AND no valid claim), no_answer_other, provider_failure. A valid final 'Answer: N' claim is scored correct or wrong regardless of stop state; the parser does not fall back to an earlier well-formed claim. Inference treats the item as the independent unit: calls are averaged within item, the 30 item means are weighted equally, and uncertainty comes from an item-clustered percentile bootstrap (10,000 draws, seed 20260713) that resamples items while carrying all of a selected item's calls, so 150 calls never become 150 independent problems. Unrepeated proportions get exact Clopper-Pearson intervals instead. Tail statistics were gated by item count before collection: median/p90/p95/max need 20 items, p99 needs 100, 90%-CVaR needs 50, so the paper refuses to report p99 and CVaR even though the software could compute them. Separately, a July 14 documentation/Models-API census of seven model IDs and 19 preregistered raw-response probes on July 16 tested echoed effort, thinking-block structure and explicit disabled-thinking requests, with an evidence hierarchy under which an absent thinking block plus zero thinking tokens stays 'documentation grade' because it cannot distinguish disabled thinking from adaptive thinking that chose zero. Prompt, parser, taxonomy, statistical rules, contract registry, spending ceilings and analysis pipeline were frozen and SHA-256 pinned before any registered outcome was inspected.

## Results

Primary registered contrast: mean delivered cost was $0.01031 per call higher under explicit high than under omitted, 95% item-clustered bootstrap CI [+$0.00204, +$0.01974] -- an interval excluding zero, so the cost difference was detected. The paired accuracy contrast was +0.0133 with CI [-0.0267, +0.0467]: no accuracy difference detected, but the interval still permits a gain of up to 4.67 percentage points, which the paper insists must not be read as 'high effort buys nothing'. Cell values: Sonnet high 0.927 accuracy (139/150 calls) at $0.08029 mean cost/call [$0.05107, $0.11587]; Sonnet omitted 0.913 (137/150) at $0.06998 [$0.04427, $0.10062]. Cost per correct answer $0.08665 under high and $0.07662 under omitted -- registered point estimates with no separately registered interval, so the ordering is not an inferential claim. Medians were nearly identical ($0.04169 high vs $0.04093 omitted) while maxima differed ($0.58653 vs $0.53290), i.e. the mean gap sits in the upper tail rather than the typical call. Descriptively, 141/150 explicit-high calls and 140/150 omitted calls returned positive reasoning-token counts (positive-call medians 3,359 vs 3,133.5 tokens), so omission was not acting as disabled thinking; the paper flags these as post hoc and not evidence of equivalence. Reference cells: GPT-5.6 Terra omitted 28/30 correct [0.779, 0.992] at $0.02319/call, cost/correct $0.02485; Claude Fable 5 omitted 30/30 [0.884, 1.000] at $0.21582/call -- roughly 8.7x Terra's cost for at most 6.7 points of accuracy, with overlapping intervals, so the cost-per-correct ordering (Terra < Sonnet omitted < Sonnet high < Fable) is explicitly not a dominance claim. The 5-item July 9 bridge had gpt-5.4-mini low and high both at 4/5 correct with costs $0.01006 and $0.04082, i.e. 4x the cost for identical observed accuracy, but on five items and non-contemporaneous. The preregistered conservative gate on rail exhaustion fired: no main-grid call ended in no_answer_rail and none reached 99% rail utilization (Sonnet high 7/150 reached 50%, 1/150 reached 90%; Sonnet omitted 4/150 at 50%, 0 at 90%), so the preliminary full-rail failure mode did not generalize, and the zero-event bootstrap intervals that collapse to [0.0000, 0.0000] are explicitly declared uninformative. Within-item variance is large: on item 11, Sonnet high spanned $0.000648 to $0.391888 across five calls and mixed wrong with correct outcomes, while Sonnet omitted produced five identical wrong answers all at $0.000648. Sonnet omitted had 4 mixed-outcome items, Sonnet high 3. Descriptive latency on the first-20-item sequential subsample only: median 7.8s Terra, 16.7s Sonnet high, 17.1s Sonnet omitted, 17.8s Fable (Fable p95 226.1s, max 482.9s). Total study spend was $33.043144, reconciled to provider dashboards at cent granularity for the main session. Probe findings: omission semantics differ across models and within one provider -- GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna raw-echoed reasoning.effort=medium when omitted, Fable 5 defaults to high with adaptive thinking always on and returns HTTP 400 to an explicit disable request, while Sonnet 5 and Opus 4.8 returned no thinking block and zero thinking tokens on the omitted probe, which stayed documentation-grade because it cannot separate disabled from adaptive-zero.

## Limitations

The headline contrast is weaker than 'high effort does not buy accuracy' implies, because the omitted cell's documented default is also high effort with adaptive thinking: the design contrasts an explicit request term against a default that means the same thing, not more thinking against less. That the two cells nonetheless differ in cost by a detectable $0.01031 is the finding; it does not measure the accuracy return on raising an effort ladder. Dispatch order was fixed rather than randomized (the high call always preceded the omitted call within each item/repeat pair, with bounded concurrency after the first 20 pairs), so the paper concedes it cannot separate request-form differences from dispatch-position or short-run service effects, and interprets the contrast as descriptive of the July 18 session rather than as a causal effect. Thirty curated competition-mathematics items from one task family, not a probability sample; accuracy was high in all four cells (0.913-1.000), leaving little headroom to detect a gain, which is part of why the accuracy interval is uninformative. Repeat depth is asymmetric -- five calls per item for the two Sonnet cells but one each for Terra and Fable, so no within-item variability is identified for the cross-model references. Every estimate is conditional on the served models, service products and price schedules in force on one date; the July 9 mini bridge is five items and non-contemporaneous and supports no equivalence or tail claim. Contamination is only diagnosed, not excluded: AIME 2026 was administered about a month after Anthropic's January 2026 cutoff, and the freshness diagnostic (Sonnet low answering AIME 2025 items in ~10 billed output tokens versus 755 and 1,627 tokens at matched 2026 indices) is suggestive rather than proof. Cost per correct is reported as a point estimate with no interval, so its ordering across cells cannot be tested. Billed hidden computation is measurable in volume and price but its content is unavailable, so the cost contrast cannot be attributed to any particular reasoning behaviour and no mechanism decomposition is offered. Rail exhaustion censors latent demand: the study sees the missing answer and its price, not the compute a completed response would have needed.

## Why it matters here

- **overthinking**: On topic, and unusual for the archive in that it prices the tradeoff in dollars against a preregistered statistical plan rather than in tokens against a benchmark table. The substantive result: on 30 AIME 2026 items with 150 calls per cell, asking Sonnet 5 for high reasoning effort explicitly cost $0.01031 more per call [+$0.00204, +$0.01974] than omitting the parameter, while the accuracy contrast was +0.0133 [-0.0267, +0.0467] -- a detected price difference with no detected accuracy difference, and cost per correct answer worse under high ($0.08665 vs $0.07662). That is the overthinking pattern stated as a purchase. Two qualifications matter for how the archive should cite it. First, and the paper is explicit about this while its title is not: Sonnet 5's documented default is already high effort with adaptive thinking, so the two cells differ in whether high is stated or defaulted, not in how much thinking was requested -- confirmed by 140/150 omitted calls returning positive reasoning tokens at a median of 3,133.5. This is therefore not evidence that a high effort setting fails to buy accuracy over a low one; it is evidence that a nominally null request-form change moves realized cost. Second, the design is underpowered for the accuracy question by construction: all four cells score 0.913-1.000, so there is little headroom, and the authors say so and refuse to read the null as absence of benefit. What generalizes best is methodological. The insistence that wrong answers and rail-exhausted no-answers stay inside the cost total as purchased outcomes is directly applicable to any efficiency claim in this topic, where a method that saves tokens by failing is easy to mis-score. So is the item-clustered bootstrap that stops five repeats per item from being counted as five problems, and the preregistered refusal to report p99 or CVaR at n=30. The within-item spans are the sharpest raw observation: on item 11, five calls under a single fixed contract ranged from $0.000648 to $0.391888 and mixed wrong with correct, so per-call reasoning length under an identical request is dispersed by nearly three orders of magnitude -- any stopping rule evaluated on a single sample per item is measuring noise. Finally, the probe census documents that 'omit the effort parameter' resolves to medium on GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna but to high on Fable 5 and Sonnet 5, including within one provider, which means cross-paper comparisons of 'default reasoning effort' are not comparing the same thing.

## Abstract

API buyers purchase a dated contract, not a model name alone: the contract includes the requested and served model, reasoning-effort term or its omission, output rail, service product, prompt, and price schedule. We study the reasoning-effort term through a registered paired contrast of Sonnet 5 with explicit high effort against the same model with effort omitted, using 30 AIME 2026 items and five calls per item. Every paid attempt was assigned one frozen terminal category, and inference resampled items while retaining their repeated calls. Mean delivered cost was \$0.01031 per call higher under the explicit-high contract than under the omitted contract [+\$0.00204, +\$0.01974]. The corresponding accuracy contrast was +0.0133 [-0.0267, +0.0467]; we did not detect an accuracy difference, and the interval permits a gain of up to 4.67 percentage points that this design cannot rule out. Cost per correct answer was \$0.08665 under the high-effort contract and \$0.07662 under the omitted contract, as registered point estimates. A dated contract census, Models-API metadata, and preregistered raw-response probes further documented model-specific omission semantics, including within a provider; claims remained at documentation grade when raw structure was indeterminate. The request registry, parser, terminal taxonomy, statistical plan, and analysis pipeline were frozen before outcomes were examined; the resulting claims are bounded to the model, task, and collection date studied.
